entries.title: Trident (Trishula)
entries.description: A three-pronged spear carried by Shiva and by Durga in many images. Shailputri and Mahagauri hold it.
entries.significance: Often read as power over the three gunas, the three times (past, present, future) or the three worlds. Interpretations differ.

entries.title: Lotus (Padma)
entries.description: A flower that grows in mud and rises clean above the water. Several Devis hold or sit on a lotus.
entries.significance: A common symbol of purity, spiritual growth and detachment from surroundings.

entries.title: Crescent moon
entries.description: A half-moon worn in the hair of Shiva and on the brow of Shailputri and Chandraghanta.
entries.significance: Linked with calm, with the passing of time and with the mind at rest.

entries.title: Japa mala
entries.description: A string of beads used to count repetitions of a name or mantra. Brahmacharini holds one in her right hand.
entries.significance: Represents steady practice and concentration; the discipline of repetition.

entries.title: Kamandalu
entries.description: A small water pot traditionally carried by sages and ascetics.
entries.significance: Stands for simplicity and for having only what is needed. It also belongs to Brahmacharini's iconography.

entries.title: Bell (Ghanta)
entries.description: Bells are rung in Hindu temples to begin worship. Chandraghanta takes her name from a bell-shaped moon.
entries.significance: The sound is said to welcome the divine and to clear the mind of distraction. This is a devotional interpretation.

entries.title: Sword (Khadga)
entries.description: A weapon shown in several forms of Durga, including Katyayani and Kalaratri.
entries.significance: Often understood as discernment that cuts through ignorance, as well as the power to defend justice.

entries.title: Conch (Shankha)
entries.description: A shell blown as a horn in rituals. It appears in the hands of Siddhidatri.
entries.significance: Its sound announces auspicious beginnings and is linked with the primordial sound Om.

entries.title: Discus (Chakra)
entries.description: A spinning disc held by Siddhidatri, and by Vishnu as the Sudarshana Chakra.
entries.significance: Represents the cycle of time and the turning of dharma.

entries.title: Mace (Gada)
entries.description: A heavy club shown in the hands of Kushmanda and Siddhidatri.
entries.significance: Symbolises strength used with purpose, and the removal of obstacles.

entries.title: Lion
entries.description: The traditional mount of Durga, and of several of her Navadurga forms, including Chandraghanta, Kushmanda, Skandamata and Katyayani.
entries.significance: Courage and sovereignty under control; power that serves protection.

entries.title: Bull (Nandi)
entries.description: The white bull associated with Shiva. Shailputri and Mahagauri ride one.
entries.significance: Steadiness and devotion. It is a reminder of their connection to Shiva.

entries.title: Donkey (Gardabha)
entries.description: The mount described for Kalaratri.
entries.significance: Often read as humility: even the least admired creature can carry the goddess. Devotional interpretations vary.

entries.title: Abhaya mudra
entries.description: A raised open palm held toward the viewer. Many images of the Devis show it.
entries.significance: Means 'do not fear'. It is a gesture of protection and reassurance.

entries.title: Varada mudra
entries.description: An open palm turned downward, with fingers pointing down.
entries.significance: The gesture of giving: blessings and boons offered to devotees.

entries.title: Shakti
entries.description: The Sanskrit word for power or energy, understood in many Hindu traditions as the dynamic divine feminine principle.
entries.significance: In Shakta traditions Shakti is the ultimate reality; in other traditions she is the active power of a god. Navratri celebrates her.

entries.title: The number nine
entries.description: Navratri lasts nine nights and honours nine forms of the goddess.
entries.significance: Nine is the number of completion in many Indian systems of counting. Some traditions link it to nine planets or nine kinds of devotion, but interpretations vary.

entries.title: Kalasha (sacred pot)
entries.description: A pot filled with water, topped with leaves and a coconut. Many households install one at the start of Navratri; Kushmanda holds a similar pot of nectar.
entries.significance: Signifies abundance, life and the presence of the divine in the pot.

entries.title: Garba and Dandiya
entries.description: Circle dances of Gujarat danced during the nine nights, with sticks in dandiya.
entries.significance: The circle is often explained as the cycle of life, around a central light that represents the goddess. Dance becomes an offering.

entries.title: Vijayadashami
entries.description: The tenth day, after the nine nights, celebrated as Dussehra in many regions.
entries.significance: Marks the victory of good over evil: Durga's victory over Mahishasura in some regions and Rama's victory over Ravana in others.
